displayQuote: Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction

meta.title: Who really said "Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — this really is Ronald Reagan. He used it in his 1961 Phoenix Chamber of Commerce speech and again in his 1967 California inaugural.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Reagan: documented in his 1961 Phoenix Chamber of Commerce address and his 1967 California gubernatorial inaugural.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Reagan line. Its fuller form — “Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction. We didn’t pass it on to our children in the bloodstream…” — is documented in his 30 March 1961 address to the Phoenix Chamber of Commerce ↗, and the exact phrase reappears in his 5 January 1967 California gubernatorial inaugural ↗: “Freedom is a fragile thing and is never more than one generation away from extinction.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Address to the Phoenix Chamber of Commerce

source.excerpt: Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction. We didn’t pass it on to our children in the bloodstream. The only way they can inherit the freedom we have known is if we fight for it, protect it, defend it, and then hand it to them with the well fought lessons of how they in their lifetime must do the same.
trail: Wikiquote lists this in its sourced section ↗, tracing the fuller wording to the 30 March 1961 Phoenix Chamber of Commerce address.
The California State Library’s archive of the 5 January 1967 inaugural ↗ contains the exact phrase verbatim.
The Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation ↗ also catalogs the line, citing his later 6 July 1987 Kiwanis International remarks.
The Human Trafficking Institute’s ‘InContext’ piece ↗ reproduces the fuller 1961 passage in context.
source.excerptNote: The fuller 1961 wording as recorded in Wikiquote’s sourced section. In the 1967 California inaugural the phrase is embedded in a single sentence: “Freedom is a fragile thing and is never more than one generation away from extinction.”
source.rightsHolder: Estate of Ronald Reagan / Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation & Institute
source.rightsNote: The line comes from Reagan speeches delivered in 1961 and 1967 — both well after 1931 — so the text is in copyright in the United States, with rights held by the Reagan estate and the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation & Institute. The underlying idea is free to quote and discuss; the specific speech text is not public domain.

author.name: Ronald Reagan
author.heading: About Ronald Reagan
author.bio: Ronald Reagan was a Hollywood actor turned conservative political figure who served as Governor of California (1967–1975) and as the 40th President of the United States (1981–1989). Known as “the Great Communicator,” he returned repeatedly to the theme that liberty is not self-sustaining but must be actively defended by each generation — a message he first road-tested on the corporate speaking circuit in the early 1960s before carrying it into elected office.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This quote is correctly credited to Reagan — the honest caveat here is about which speech and which wording, not who said it.

items.why: The line is variously dated to the 1961 Phoenix Chamber of Commerce speech ↗, the 1967 California inaugural, or his 1987 Kiwanis remarks. All three are real; 1961 is the earliest documented use.

The compact meme form — just the first sentence — drops Reagan’s “we didn’t pass it on… in the bloodstream” continuation, and the 1967 version actually reads “Freedom is a fragile thing and is never more than one generation away from extinction,” per the California State Library text ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: this is authentically Ronald Reagan — documented in his 1961 Phoenix speech and 1967 inaugural ↗ — and one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives scrutiny intact.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Reagan built the line during his years as a traveling spokesman for General Electric in the late 1950s and early 1960s, when he honed a stump speech on the fragility of liberty. By the time he ran for and won the California governorship, the phrase had become a signature.

Its enduring appeal is that it reframes freedom not as a possession but as an inheritance that can lapse in a single handoff — a warning that has been echoed by later figures, including a 2018 speech by French President Emmanuel Macron who quoted it almost verbatim.
context.pull: “We didn’t pass it on to our children in the bloodstream.”
